The licence is fine, but the TEE keygen failed. Scan still works and emits a DEGRADED token: unattested, signed with a software key if one is available, carrying the detector findings and the reason the keygen failed.\n\nTap Scan to see what the backend receives.
The licence blob did not parse at all. That is the one failure that cannot emit even a degraded token, because the server public key lives inside that blob.

what a backend stores per session
No scan in memory. Run Initialize, then Scan, and open this screen from the results.
No session established yet. A steady-state scan needs the facts the bootstrap scan returned - run Initialize, then Scan.

This token carries no hardware binding. It is unauthenticated - anyone able to encrypt to the server key could mint one naming any session - so it is never evidence of a clean device. It is evidence that something stopped this device binding itself, which is worth strictly more than the silence this case used to produce.
This token is bound to a hardware-attested key. The chain is what the backend grades; the level below only says a chain exists.
`key` describes the key, `signed by` what actually signed THIS token. They degrade independently: a hooked keygen gives NONE/SOFTWARE, a device that lost its keystore mid-session gives the reverse.
Is this a bug or an injection?
both look identical at a glance, so the backend classifies on two axes
1. The reason. A device fault reports a known sub-code such as strongbox_unavailable:-68. An EMPTY detail means nothing threw - the binding just never appeared, which is hook-shaped.

2. Corroboration. The detectors run first and never touch the TEE, so their findings are independent evidence about this same process. A hook that broke the attestation usually trips them; a StrongBox that was never fitted trips nothing. Check the Signals screen.

The detail above is self-reported and unsigned on a degraded token, so a benign-looking reason can never clear a device on its own. Degraded tokens incriminate reliably; they exonerate only in aggregate.

An AUTHENTICITY failure means the token is a proven forgery - nothing in it is usable, and the verdict is REJECT. A DEVICE INTEGRITY failure means the token is genuine but the device honestly reports an untrustworthy state, which is COMPROMISED rather than forged.
The order is the order they ran. It is the audit trail for this decision.

No detector fired. That is NOT evidence of a clean device: every core here fails open, so a core that cannot read its input contributes nothing rather than a guess. Absence of a signal means nothing was affirmatively found, and no more than that.
Each signal is an opaque code on the wire - the detector and kind are resolved here from the registry. Severity is a device HINT; the backend decides what blocks.
This code is retired and should never arrive. The registry that resolved it is out of date.
No row in this build\'s catalogue. The registry has moved on — regenerate it.
Confirmed hook pool: the stubs in this region branch into real code. RWX on its own is ambiguous - an ART JIT cache is RWX too - so this is the field that separates a hook from a cache.
Definitive hook - the structural and behavioural checks agree on: %1$s. Either alone is weaker; agreeing is the finding.
Confirmed RWX hook pool: %1$d region(s) whose stubs branch into real code.

This scan carried no fingerprint. Only the bootstrap scan sends the full set; a steady-state scan sends its digest alone, because an OS update cannot happen inside one session - so a digest that changes mid-session means the device changed under it.
These are already the peppered SHA-256 digests the backend stores. The raw Widevine id and ANDROID_ID never leave the handset, so what is shown here is the opaque form, truncated only for legibility.

device: Widevine-rooted. Survives a reinstall, and is expected to survive a flash - Widevine provisioning lives in the DRM keybox rather than /data. That expectation has not been tested on a flashed handset.
app: ANDROID_ID. Survives a reinstall, resets on a flash.

build, kernel and patch are read NATIVELY - system properties and a raw uname syscall - not through the JVM. They feed the patch cross-check, and reading spoofer-detection evidence through the surface a spoofer hooks would defeat it.
A missing fingerprint never blocks a scan. This is a fraud-correlation input, not an integrity gate.

Attestation runs ONCE, at setSession, so these facts have to outlive it. The verifier keeps no state of its own: a bootstrap scan returns them, the caller stores them on its own session record, and hands them back on every later scan. That is what keeps the backend stateless.
Staleness is judged on the OLDEST of the three: a current framework patch on a two-year-old bootloader is still exposed.
